rule_outcome: plain chat is at least as good

reasons: X captures realistic second-round effects (foreign makers repricing below the cap, later FX shock, customs revenue recovering via quota). Y is numerically tighter but has a static environment and end-of-game artifacts (stockpiling or expanding because it is the last stage).

Y's actors visibly react to each other and to thresholds (consumers delay, then grey market, then protest; government waits, then gives a quota). X unwinds the ban too smoothly, and its stage-5 currency shock barely moves the numbers.

X shows the ban leaking through below-threshold models and foreign makers, supply recovering while FX pressure ends higher, defeating the ban's purpose. Y is careful but muted, with a passive environment and small numeric responses to the quota.

X shows a turning point: a downturn on top of free AI leads to contract cuts, layoffs and emigration, then a niche for complex and review work. Y is a smooth, shock-free glide where developers upskill every stage and employment barely moves.

X's numbers track the actions closely, and its shocks (code failure, downturn, rival going free) cascade into rate cuts, junior layoffs and emigration. Y is a flat, monotone drift. Its environment never acts and developers repeat the same action five times.

X has turning points: a trust shock, a downturn, junior layoffs, emigration, and complex work staying outsourced. Y is a smooth, repetitive erosion where developers upskill every stage and the environment never moves.

X stress-tests the plan with rumour, heat, a pipe burst and rain, and shows anger peaking when the tariff hike coincides with the burst. Y has no events at all, flat health risk, and tanker hikes driven by last-stage logic.

X has realistic shocks (rumour, heat wave, pipe burst, rain), an anger peak followed by easing, and a steady drain on the utility budget, all with closely matching numbers. Y is static, health risk sits flat, and the actors give meta 'last stage' reasons.

X adds plausible drought shocks (rumour, heat, pipe burst, rain), shows the tariff anger spike and steady budget drain, and lets rain open the way to easing. Y keeps the environment idle and has end-of-horizon artefacts in tanker and household moves.

Y shows escalation (panic buying, blockades, ports), shelf depletion and prices staying high after the deal. X keeps shelves full throughout a nationwide strike, settles within days, and then has two empty stages where every actor holds.

Y shows escalation (panic buying, blockades, ports), rationing and price hikes, then a deal after which prices stay high: a useful finding that prices do not fall back. X's strike ends quickly with shelves barely touched, and stages 4-5 are all holds.

Y shows the real risks: panic buying, a blockade, escalation to the ports, and prices that stay high after the deal. X settles fast, shelves barely move despite halved freight, and the last two stages are all holds.
